Jobs to be Done

SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 6

Given June 30th, 2024 by Yonatan Stern


So, first of all, thank you all for showing up. We are expanding our audience in here from an age perspective. So the youngest one today is three months old, and he promised to be quiet and ask questions only in English. So there is a change, a little bit of a change. There was a request for people to mingle and meet one another. So what we're going to do is before the break — we have a half an hour break in the middle — we will have three people introduce themselves for a minute or two minutes, short. So those of you who want to come and present for a minute or two minutes, three people. So at the end, I will ask who wants to come. And those of you who want, just raise your hands and we'll pick the first three.

And we are very fortunate to be in lecture number six. We covered already a lot of ground, and we're going to continue building the concept of how you build successful companies. So, again, what is the SmartUp Academy? This is a program to teach the profession. As I've said many times, building a company is a profession. There is a lot of stuff that somebody needs to know when they build a company. And I've tried to organize it in a way that can describe and make sense. And with that, we build successful companies. And we have a definition. What is a successful company? So a successful company has three elements. Number one, it is profitable. Profitable. Profit. A company is not grown up until it generates cash, month after month.

If it's not generating cash, it relies on investors. And investors have the tendency to be there when you don't need them and not be there when you need them. So, all right, those of you with experience can attest to the validity of this data. So when you are making money, you don't have to worry about it. You are making money by yourself. The best investors ever — called customers. Second, if you build the company correctly, you can grow really fast. We talk about it a lot. Ideas like branding first and other ideas on how to grow. And the last element is that all of that can be done with modest investment. If you build the company correctly, you don't need a lot of money. What does it mean, not a lot of money? Raises from a few hundred thousand dollars, two, three, maybe four million dollars. That's it, basically.

What is needed to build a successful company if it is built correctly. We also have workshops in here. So a lot of these ideas I talk about in very general terms. Essentially, each company has its own unique problems or challenges. So we also have a program where a small number of companies can sit around the table and we discuss their specific needs. Obviously, if we talk about branding or marketing, then all the companies participate in talking about branding and marketing. If we talk about cash flow, then all of them talk. And the end is the residency program. The reason I put in here the picture of a hospital is obvious. Students finish six years in medical school, high degrees, established, right on the dean's list. And nobody will dare go to their doctor until they spend four or five years in a hospital.

Because clearly what you learn in school and reality are just not the same. So what we're doing here is not very different. I can tell you everything you want to hear and I can explain it and give examples and give homework. When it comes to your own company, it just looks different because every company is unique. It's not the same. And you are going to do exactly what I said not to do. Why? Because that's the way we all work. So we have a residency program. We sit with these companies that are in the program once a week, once every two, three weeks, depending on the situation, and go over all the operations of the company. Strategy. Again, this is just to remind people what we talked about before, about moving from science to business.

I've talked about Galileo Galilei, who said mathematics is the language in which the universe is written. Which means at the end of the day, everything has to be written in equations, in numbers. If they don't, then you can't make decisions, you can't predict, you can't do anything. And the language of business is very simple. And to deal with money, we build spreadsheets. We spent about one full lecture and another part of a lecture to show how we built this model. Very, very important. We're going to review it from time to time in the following lectures and show how everything we talk about is reflected in those spreadsheets. And how we can measure success. So we have three pillars of successful companies. How do we measure that? Okay, so how do we measure profitability?

The measure that we put into this model is how long does it take for the company to become profitable? When I say profitable, I mean cash generating — not P&L, but cash generating, month after month. So does it take you three months, six months, 12 months, three years, 10 years? That's the measure of profitability that we put in place. Modest investment — how much money you need before you can turn profitable. And last but not least, fast growing. The way we calculate fast growing is to think about this as an investor. So if you invest in real estate and you put $2 million in real estate, you ask yourself, when am I going to get my money back?

Right.

So you want your money back. Same should be with startups. So when you build a company, if your family puts half a million dollars in you, they want it back and they want it back fast. So that's a good measure of how successful your company is. So these are the three measurements. This is how we calculate them. So every time you build a very complicated spreadsheet with a lot of assumptions and everything, at the end you calculate just three numbers. How long it took you to become profitable, how much money you have to put in the business till you reach profitability, and how long does it take you to return the investment. That's all from your entire spreadsheet. And that would allow you to compare assumptions. Well, if the price is $2,000 versus $1,000, what difference does it make down here?

If I charge, as I showed before, $12,000 a year upfront or $1,000 a month, it's a huge difference in the amount of money you make. Huge difference. So assumptions like that should be tested. In simple terms, a business model is basically — how is your company going to make money? At the end of the day, people say, well, we want to do something disruptive, we're going to change the world, blah, blah. Okay, do that on your own time on the weekend. When you build a company and people give you money, they want money back. It's that simple. When you build a company and you don't have a rich father, you need the company to make money or else your wife might be angry. So it's really simple. But building a company is a very complex combination of parameters.

Product, the service, customer profile, pricing, a gazillion things that need to be taken into account. And that's what we're doing here in the lectures. We basically slice each aspect of how you build the company, analyze it, give you some principles, and show you what works and what doesn't work. Really critical — a company gets its DNA very early. And the DNA is obviously the DNA of the founder, but also the DNA of the business model that you choose at every stage. Doing a pivot two years later is extremely expensive and complicated. So you better think a lot about the business model, do a lot of tests and trials and learning before you make those decisions, because they are very costly if you make a mistake. When you can test them, I will show how you can test them. And it's usually a process.

So you make some decisions. You go, you test them in the market. When I say test them in the market, it's testing with potential customers or customers, because at the end of the day, all you want is a lot of money from your customers. So it's very easy to see — if I charge this, do I get it? If I package it this way, do I get more customers or less customers? So what do you need to know when you build a business model? You really want to answer all the W-H questions. So the first question is, who are your users? And the second question, which we're going to talk about today, is what problems do users try to solve? The language that is used in this presentation today is "Jobs to be Done."

I'll explain later on who coined the term and how it evolved. But really, this is the main thing that we're going to discuss today — Jobs to be Done. Which basically means what's the problem you're trying to solve, really, for the customers? And even though it sounds like a pretty simple question, as you will see, this is a fairly complicated question — what problems are you trying to solve? Who pays for it? Really critical. And when I say who pays for it, you will realize later on in one of my lectures that actually there are a lot of models of who pays for it. And it might even be as subtle as the employee enjoys, the company pays. It's a very different behavior than the company pays the company's expenses. So there are a lot of differences. What exactly do they pay for?

So pretty much in a lot of products, you can parse it in different ways. The most obvious one is the coffee machine over there. The coffee machine costs very little money, but the capsules cost a lot of money. So what do you pay for? You could have said, you know, the machine itself is very expensive and the capsules are cheap. They reverse it. We all know that there are all of these business models where they pull you in with cheap prices and you pay the cost later on. Where do they pay? It sounds stupid. Well, the question is really, do they pay on the web where you go click a button and pay with a credit card? Or do they talk to a salesperson? Do they do a wire transfer? All of these things have a big impact on your ability to sell at scale.

How much do they pay? Obviously. When do they pay? As I said before, $12,000 upfront or $1,000 a month? Do they pay before they get the product? Do they pay net 60, net 90? All of these questions have huge impact on your cash flow and therefore profitability and so forth and so on. Okay, so I promised you that this time I'm going to talk about somebody else, not just me. So — it's Clayton Christensen. I introduced him last time.

He was a professor at Harvard Business School. Before that he was a businessman. He built a company, then he decided he wanted to do research. He did his PhD at Harvard and then he became a professor. And he did some very interesting research on why good companies that are very successful fail many times when a new technology or a new process comes on board and they let competitors take the market away from them. And his main insight was — they are not idiots. They didn't build a company worth billions of dollars by being idiots. So they are not idiots. They see the threat. They see what's going on in the market, and somehow, stupidly, supposedly, they don't react correctly. They don't do anything about it. Why? What's going on?

And his conclusion, which is very —
competitors take the market away from. And his main insight was they are not idiots. They didn't build a company worth billions of dollars by being idiots. So they are not idiots. They see the threat. They see what's going on in the market, and somehow, stupidly, supposedly, they don't react correctly. They don't do anything about it. Why? What's going on?

And his conclusion, which is very interesting — I'll not talk about it this time, but maybe in the next lecture. His insight was that they do what they are supposed to do, which is increase profits. So what happens is that as competitors come in, they move upstream to products with a higher margin and they kind of drop down the products that don't have a high margin. They just needed to deal with it because customers wanted it. So if a competitor comes in at the low end of the market, they very happily shed off these product lines, leave them for the competition, and then the competition from below basically fills up. It's a little bit more elaborate. I will talk about it next time. The reason I put all the videos in here is there are plenty of videos on the web. I strongly recommend watching them.

He's also funny. He's kind of British. So he has British jokes. But he's very funny and very interesting. Spend some time with him. So the book I'm going to talk about is called The Innovator's Solution, because the previous book was called The Innovator's Dilemma. So if you have a dilemma, this is the solution. And what he's talking about is the following. This is the book in Hebrew. I found that it is in Hebrew. I don't know that you can really find it, but there is the book and this is what it says: understanding customers does not drive innovation success. Understanding customer jobs does. So this entire concept, and we will talk about it in great length later on, is that really this concept that you need to understand what the customer needs is wrong.

You have to look at what are they trying to accomplish, analyze it, and then build your products to deal with the root cause, not when they say, "Oh yeah, I like this course." Okay, so I decided that this time I will confess to all my sins and tell you stories from two of my companies and how I experienced these jobs to be done firsthand, because I didn't know that it's called jobs to be done. It was just painful, but I learned the hard way. So what he's talking about — the company was, that's the second company I built, was founded in 1984 and we had investors that are legendary for those of you who are beyond 20 years old. The first one was Uzia Galil, who created Elron. Elron was the parent of Elbit. So Elbit is two words, Elron and Bitachon.

So it was a joint venture between Elron and the Ministry of Defense. Athena Ventures — then he worked with us, with Dan Tolkowsky. Dan Tolkowsky was a pilot. He was the head of the Air Force many years ago. Then he was the CEO of Discount Investment. And then he started a venture capital, the first venture capital in Israel, Athena Ventures. And the first fund was $40 million. And we were very fortunate to be one of the first companies. But then we raised a lot of money, about $12 million. So what's the product? At the time we're talking now about '84. There was also AI. So AI came in waves. For those of you who are old enough, you have seen the ups and downs. You have to say that this time the AI is for real, the other time it's not for real.

And this one is really for real. And at the time it was called Expert Systems. An Expert System is essentially a set of if-then rules. If you see this, then do this. If you see this, then do that. Basically it's just a list of rules. The same way that you describe to a kid what to do or to a pupil what to do. That's the way you describe it. Just give a list of rules on how to do it. The systems were a little bit more sophisticated. So the sequence was not important, it was more interesting. But the idea that we had was there are companies — and I'll give you our customers — companies like Xerox, Philips Medical, Applied Materials, Varian. Those of you who recognize the last three — these are companies that deal with equipment to produce integrated circuits, chips.

So they have very sophisticated, complicated equipment. When it fails, the technician has to come in and fix it. Usually the technician has no clue what the machine really does, but it's very complicated. So he starts swapping boards. Every board costs about twenty, thirty thousand dollars. It's a very expensive process. Just swap boards and sort them back. And also, many times they don't catch the real problem. So what we decided to do is build an expert system where we work with the client and we take all the knowledge of the best engineers, put it into this expert system, and when a technician goes to the field, they have a tool that gives them guidance and advice how to identify the problem and how to fix it. Great idea.

The interesting thing is, as a condition for getting the funding, the investors did the right thing, which is send us out to the US to meet with potential customers, interview them, write down the summary of the interview and bring them back, showing that customers are really interested in this solution. So we went, we talked to these companies and others as well. We, I think, went to about 12 companies and were very encouraged. People said, this is really great. It's a huge solution for us. It's a really expensive problem. Yes, go ahead and do it. We asked, would you be my customer? They said, absolutely, sure, yes. Okay. So as part of that, we founded the company in '84. I moved to the US because most of our customers were in the US in '89. And the company continually grew.

So by 1992, it brought in four and a half million dollars in revenues. Nice. There's only one problem — we were never profitable. So if you think I'm nuts about profitability, this is the reason. When you are not profitable, you have to raise money round after round from investors. It's very painful. So one day I talked to one of our bigger customers and I asked him a thorny question, because parallel to us there was another company that started about the same time. And that company, what they built was just a basic CRM for the field service engineers. So if there was a call, they would put it in the CRM. They also put the inventory of the parts in there. The parts — mainly the spare parts — were usually in the trunk of the car because the customers were all over.

So the engineers would go by car, and in the trunk they have a lot of replacement parts. And so they wanted to keep track of where these parts are. And this company started about the same time as us. We were four and a half million, they were 25 million. And that really bothered me. So I went to a customer that I knew. Can you explain to me why do you spend so much money on them and so little money on us? So he said to me, when you came to me and you asked, is your product interesting? I said, yeah, very interesting. When you asked me, are you going to buy my product? I said, yeah, I think so. Yeah, absolutely. So I was as happy as can be. And here's what he says to me.

That was not the right question. So I said, what is the right question? So he said, the right question you should have asked me is: if you only have $100,000 in your budget, would you buy the product — an artificial intelligence system — or would you buy something else? And I said, why? Why would you buy something else? And he said, very simple. Because in each car of my engineers, in the trunk, they have hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of spare parts. I have no clue where this is. I have $50 million in spare parts. Where? I don't know where it is because it travels around the country. And so I want to know where everything is and I want to make sure that if somebody who is 10 miles away has it, they can switch it.

So it is far more important for me than your nice product. A nice product is a future product. But right now I have real problems right now. Jobs to be done. I asked about the wrong job. If I had asked, if you only have that amount of money, what would you buy? Chances are we would have developed something else. Not expensive, not artificial intelligence, not disruptive technology, just simple CRM networks. That's a very important message. Okay, so jobs to be done is look at the situation from the customer's perspective, not yours. My perspective was I'm an engineer. I was ahead of my time. I'm not going to deal with CRMs, I'm disruptive, blah, blah. I left the artificial intelligence systems company in 1992. Swore to God the next company I'm going to do will be profitable as fast as possible. Thank God I did.

But yes, that's the lesson I learned. Any questions? Okay, so I'll go now to the foundational story. If you listen to Christensen, that's the story he's going to tell. It's a really interesting story. I didn't write anything on the slide because it's a long story, but it's a very interesting story. So the guys — Christensen is already a well-known author and a well-known consultant. And McDonald's hired them to do something interesting. They sell milkshakes at their stores and they tried to improve or increase the sales of the milkshakes. And they tried to do this, do that, add chocolate, take chocolate, add sugar, take sugar. Nothing makes any difference. And so they said, here we have this very smart guy, let's have him check it. Okay?

So they go to some stores and they sit there from 7 o'clock in the morning till 9 at night, 18 hours a day. And they write down every customer that comes in. At what time did they come? Was it a male, a female? At what age? How were they dressed? What did they do with the milkshake? Did they take it and run away? Did they sit there and drink it at the store? What did they do? Literally, customer by customer in a few stores, just write down like anthropologists. And they discovered some interesting patterns. There were actually two very different populations that bought milkshakes. One population came in the morning from 7 o'clock in the morning till about 9 in the morning. They were all dressed like me — suit and tie, whatever — took the milkshake, paid and went out.

That was it. Took it, went out. Then in the afternoon there was a different audience, different clientele that came. Usually mothers with kids, after they took them from school, they come, they buy food, they buy milkshake and they sit with the kid and they eat the meal. Two different audiences, two different dynamics. So the following day or two days later, they decide they're going to track these people and find out what's going on here. So they start with the morning, and when this nice gentleman or lady runs out of the store, they say, give me a moment, talk to me please. Yeah, why did you buy the milkshake? So I wanted a drink. Yeah, what else? Why did you buy it? And they said, what does it do for you?

And they said, well, you know, I'm going in the car, I drive to work. So I needed something to keep myself busy and I need something filling. And if you didn't have milkshake, what would you do? Oh, well, I tried bananas, but you know, they don't fill you up. And what else? So I tried to buy donuts, but you know, I'm on a diet, I can't eat donuts. And it also leaves crumbs on my suit. It's not good. What else did you try? Gradually, when they started asking a lot of questions — simple questions — what happens if you don't have it? What do you do? And so forth. They realized that the job of this milkshake was: I have now a half an hour commute.
And what else? So I tried to buy donuts, but, you know, I'm on a diet, I think donuts. And it also leaves crumbs on my suit. It's not good. What else did you try? Gradually, when they started asking a lot of questions, stupid questions — what happens if you don't have it? What do you do? And so forth. They realize that the job of this job student was: I have now a half an hour commute.

I'm not hungry yet, but I know I'm going to be hungry about 10 o'clock in the morning, so I want to eat something that would fill me up. I don't want something that is not healthy but full of sugar. And most of all, I only have one hand. That's all what I have — in the car I'm driving, I have one hand, and I can get myself covered with crumbs and spills. And the milkshake is just the perfect solution to all of those. I can have it with one hand. It's kind of healthy. A little bit beefy. Wonderful. Okay. In the afternoon, they called the mothers with the kids. They said, why do you buy the milkshake? They said, because we want a kid to eat something real and they want something sweet. So we have to buy them this stupid milkshake.

It's too big. They spend too much time on it. I'm stuck in here with them. I want to go home already. And they keep sucking the stupid thing. You know, they get this big cup of milk. So what do you want? Something a lot smaller.

Okay.

That will, you know, the kids will finish it quickly. A little bit more sugar, but small. Give it to me small. Okay. So they go back to McDonald's and they say you have to have two different products. The morning breakfast, you add a lot of fruits into it. You know, just chop fruit, but make it small so they go through the straw. Make the straw bigger so that they can have the fruits. And the fruit chunks are important because it makes them feel that this is healthy. Exactly. Healthy. Take the sugar down, okay. Make it more filling and more substantive. And make sure that they can take it in and out quickly. So they come in. Maybe you'll use them like coupons or something. They can come, pick it up, leave something, and go.

Okay.

So they run. They want to get out. In the afternoon, you make a very different product. Small, no straw. They need to finish it quickly. A little bit more sugar, and that's it. You can charge whatever you want. So their sales grew significantly at McDonald's. And that's the foundational story of Jobs to Be Done. So now you're as smart as I am. Any questions until now? Was it funny? All right. ZoomInfo. I promised you two stories. So this is story number two. This time I didn't leave the company. Okay. Founded in 2000. AI technology. The dog knows one trick. So one trick pony. But this time it was really much deeper. Dealt with language understanding. Dealt with a lot of stuff. You had to accept, extract information from the web. And so we needed to understand the structure of websites and services.

But this time, I was already two companies later. First was Intelligence Systems. And afterwards was Corsis. I won't talk about Corsis now. And so profitability was number one. And so we started selling. Company was started in 2000. We started selling at the end of 2001. The product was crummy. It didn't work, but I made money. So you sell what you have. And the question was, of course, what do you sell? I'll take it in a moment. A million in 2002. Three million in 2003. We became profitable towards the end of the year and six million in 2004. The company continues growing until it hit the wall. Okay, so profitability first. The market for ZoomInfo was — by the way, at that time it wasn't called ZoomInfo, it was called Eliyon. But in 2000, by 2004, it was close to being formed.

And that name remained even though it was bought by DiscoverOrg early 2019. And then they adopted ZoomInfo from me because we had a much stronger brand and much better product. So we sold to recruiters, headhunters, and HR companies. I remember I told you that the product was crummy. Let me explain what these people needed and why the crummy product was good enough for them. So what they did — let's talk about headhunters. The client comes in and says, I need a CFO for a $50 million software company. So I want somebody with experience in software in the Boston area. Find me a good candidate. We're talking now about the year 2001. No LinkedIn, no data about that. So how do you build a list of the software companies in the Boston area? $50 million and up. And their CFOs. You're stuck. That's it.

So you start calling your friends. You start building your network. That's what makes you great. Right? I'm connected. I know everybody. No, you don't. Doesn't matter. That's what you say. Come ZoomInfo and says, I can give you the list. Here's the list. Here are the software companies in Boston. Here's our estimate for sales, and here's the list of their CFOs. Done. Bang. And they took it. And they paid $1,000 a month. That was our charge at the time. And they were very happy, very excited. You see our revenue is growing. They kept growing, really fast. But big eyes. We said the market of executive recruiters and headhunters is just not big enough. There's a huge market right around the corner from you called Data for Sales and Marketing. Right.

Salespeople needed a lot more data, so they will pay a lot of money. And great. So we started selling to salespeople and they were unhappy to say the least. Very unhappy. So I started asking them, why are you not happy? They say, your product is crummy. It just doesn't work. I said, what? We have so many happy customers, and you tell me it doesn't work. It doesn't work. And then after a lot of conversations with our salespeople on the one hand, and our headhunters and recruiters on the other hand, we started realizing that these two markets were really totally different. Recruiters were looking for a needle in a haystack. They needed at the end to get one good candidate. That's it.

And in order to satisfy their clients, they needed a list of 20 that they would tell, these are the best 20 out of the 500 I looked at, blah. So all they needed is a list. They couldn't care less about phone numbers and email addresses because headhunters know how to get to people. That's not a problem. And people answered their phone calls, so that's not a problem. And so all they needed is to run the query: give me the CFOs of software companies in the Boston area, bigger than $50 million. The list was in good times 50% correct. The other 50% were bogus people. Bogus companies. Doesn't matter why, because they look at it — that's not a software company. That's stupid. They threw away all the stupid stuff, and they still stayed with enough names to make them happy.

The fact that there were no phone numbers didn't bother them, and they were as happy as they could be. We gave it to salespeople, and salespeople said, I have to make 100 phone calls a day. I call up and a man answers me and he says, that's the wrong number. How did you get there? Okay, you call this company and they say, no, we are not that company. So after about five, ten phone calls, they say, this product is stupid. Why did we buy it? So there was a little problem. The little problem was that there were no phone numbers on the internet. There were no email addresses on the internet. So if we wanted phone numbers and email addresses of people, we needed a very different source.

So one day I talked to one of my salespeople, and he says, yes, you have to see. Okay. He shows me a product and he says, well, I wanted to talk to Eyal. So I put Eyal, and look, here is the phone number and here's the email address. I said, wow, that's really cool. How do they get this? I had to share with them my address book and my email box. You did it? And they said, what do I care? You know, I said, company's email addresses — I don't care, but I get, look at all the data I get. I said, aren't you worried about sharing all of this information with other people that you don't know who they are? So we built what's called the swapper. It's a long story, I won't bore you with that.

It took us a few years to get enough people to adopt it so that we get enough data. And that's basically what all of our competitors afterwards — whether it's Apollo or Lusha or People Data Labs, I don't know. There are about 10 different competitors, part of them doing the same. Show me yours and I'll show you mine. That's about it. Okay, so but it took us years to do, and meanwhile the company was in big trouble. Literally in big trouble. We didn't lose money because I made sure we never lose money. But we were not growing and were not making money. Once we solved that problem back in 2011, 2012, the company went through the roof and the rest is history. What is Jobs to Be Done?

The theory is based on the idea that people buy products and services to accomplish specific jobs in their lives. So remember the stories I gave. So you need to understand why do they buy the product, what is really the reason they want it, and what are the alternatives they have. With Washboard, the alternative was a resume. With ZoomInfo, we didn't understand what they're going to do with it, and they had totally two different uses of it. Now these jobs can be defined in many terms. There's problem solving — like car got stuck, I have a back pain, I want to increase sales. Functional tasks — so things that have a function in their life like house cleaning, we all love house cleaning. Or managing inventory like our customers at Roche. Can be emotional needs.

I want to gain respect, you know, walking with decent gear so that when we make a video it looks nice. There are social aspects, okay, I want to dress for a party, I want to show that I'm successful. There's a very broad range of reasons or jobs that I'm trying to do. So instead of focusing on the product or the customers, which is usually how people look at the world — okay, you look at the demographics of your customers or the demographics of the product and you try to measure — what Jobs to Be Done said is don't do that. אתם משתמשים ב-Google Photos שלכם ואתם כותבים - טוב, אני לא זוכר את המספר של המכונית שלי. מסיבה כלשהי, אני לא יכול לזכור אותו. אז בכל פעם שאנשים שואלים אותי מה המספר, אני הולך ל-Google Photos ואני כותב "Lexus" ואני מקבל את המכונית שלי שצילמתי תמונה שלה. אז אני רואה את המספר. זה עובד. זה פשוט עובד.

ChatGPT.

אז כולנו חושבים על ChatGPT כמשהו שנותן לנו תשובות, אבל החמצנו את הנקודה. ChatGPT מבין את השאלה שלכם, וזה הרבה יותר חשוב מלתת לכם את התשובה. הרבה יותר חשוב, כי אני יכול להתחיל לדבר לטלוויזיה שלי ולומר, "זוכר את הסרט שראינו אתמול? אני לא זוכר את השם של השחקנים הראשיים. יש לך סרטים עם אותם שחקנים ראשיים?" והוא ייתן לי סרטים עם אותם שחקנים ראשיים. נכון? אני יכול לדבר איתו. שום דבר ממה שאמרתי זה עתה לא מסובך. יש לנו speech to text, יש לנו ChatGPT מבין. הכל נעשה. אוקיי. אני עובד עם חברה שעובדת עם לקוחות שיש להם הרבה מיקומי קמעונאות.

לכל מיקום יש הסכם שכירות שונה והם צריכים לנהל, אני לא יודע, מאות מיקומי קמעונאות, כל אחד עם מדיניות שכירות שונה, הסכם שכירות, והם רוצים לחלץ הרבה מידע מהסכמי השכירות - כמו השטח, התאריכים, המחיר למטר, מה שזה לא יהיה. הם עושים את זה ידנית. אז הם עושים רק שלושה או ארבעה פרמטרים, אבל יש אולי 20 מהם. הם פיתחו מערכת שתיקח את כל ה-20 האלה, תשים אותם ב-database ותאפשר כמה שאילתות וכולי. הנה דוגמה מצוינת. הדפסה תלת-ממדית - כולכם מודעים לזה. כמה אנשים בנו jobs to be done סביב זה? אני יודע על אחד, אבל זה לא היה לעסק. הוא בנה כפפות לאנשים עם בעיה ביד שלהם.

אז כל כפפה הייתה נעשית במיוחד לכל יד ועשה את זה עם מדפסת תלת-ממד. Drones - אני חושב ש-drones לא מנוצלים מספיק היום. אז הנה דוגמה, פשוט מראש ההר שלי. אם אתם עיר, אתם רוצים לשלוט על כל היתרי הבנייה. אנשים בונים על הגג, סוגרים מרפסות, בונים סככה בגינה. אתם רוצים לתפוס את כל זה. מה יותר קל מאשר שיהיה לכם drone פעם בשבוע שמסתובב בעיר, משווה את השבוע שעבר עם השבוע הזה ואומר לכם מי עושה מה? אז בזמן אתם מקבלים את זה. אז שוב, זה מה שאנחנו עושים וכולכם מוזמנים להצטרף אלינו. אנחנו לוקחים חופשה ליולי ואוגוסט. אז ההרצאות יחזרו ב-11 באוגוסט, אז אתם יכולים לנוח.

בינתיים, אני רוצה שתפתרו הרבה jobs to be done. ואם אתם משועממים, יש לנו עבודה בבית שלי - גינון, ניקיון, הכל. תודה רבה.
english_summary:
This lecture explores the Jobs to be Done framework as a fundamental principle for building successful companies. Yonatan Stern defines a successful company through three essential pillars: profitability measured by how quickly it generates cash month after month, the ability to grow rapidly, and achieving both with modest investment of only a few hundred thousand to a few million dollars. The emphasis is on cash generation rather than relying on unpredictable investor funding.

The core insight of Jobs to be Done is understanding what customers actually want to accomplish rather than focusing solely on technology or features. The iPod example illustrates this perfectly. While other MP3 players offered similar technology, Apple succeeded by solving the real job: people wanted easy access to music, not just a device. Steve Jobs negotiated with music publishers to create the iTunes store where any song could be purchased for 99 cents with one click. This business innovation, not technological superiority, drove success. The evolution continued logically with Spotify, which recognized that people do not want to own music, they simply want to listen to it. The same pattern emerged with Netflix for movies and e-books for reading.

A critical concept introduced is enablers, which are new technologies or business developments that make previously impossible solutions feasible. These enablers open doors for entrepreneurs to package existing technologies differently to solve specific problems. Modern enablers include speech-to-text with real-time translation, face recognition using publicly available social media data, image recognition in services like Google Photos, and ChatGPT's ability to understand natural language queries. The lecture emphasizes that most successful companies, including Amazon, Salesforce, LinkedIn, Airbnb, and Waze, achieved success without disruptive technology. Their innovation lay in identifying genuine customer needs and combining available enablers to create elegant solutions. The challenge for entrepreneurs is recognizing where these technologies can solve real problems that customers will pay for, whether through 3D printing for custom medical devices or drones for municipal building permit enforcement. Success comes from understanding jobs to be done and creatively applying available enablers.
hebrew_summary:
ההרצאה השישית בקורס יסודות SmartUp עוסקת במושג המרכזי של Jobs to be Done, שהוא אבן יסוד בהבנת איך לבנות חברות מצליחות. לפי יונתן שטרן, חברה מצליחה מתאפיינת בשלושה יסודות: רווחיות המתבטאת ביצירת מזומן חודש אחרי חודש, צמיחה מהירה המאפשרת החזר השקעה בטווח קצר, והשקעה צנועה הנעה בין מאות אלפי דולרים למספר מיליונים. כדי למדוד ולנהל את ההצלחה, חברות צריכות לבנות מודלים כספיים המחשבים כמה זמן לוקח להגיע לרווחיות, כמה כסף נדרש להשקעה, וכמה זמן לוקח להחזיר את ההשקעה למשקיעים.

המושג Jobs to be Done מתמקד בהבנה מעמיקה של מה הלקוח באמת צריך להשיג, ולא רק באיזה מוצר הוא קונה. הדוגמה המרכזית בהרצאה היא סיפור האיפוד של אפל. למרות שנגני MP3 היו קיימים כבר בשנות התשעים, הם נכשלו כי לא פתרו את הבעיה האמיתית. אפל הבינה שהלקוחות לא רצו רק להקשיב למוזיקה, אלא גם להשיג אותה בקלות. החדשנות האמיתית של סטיב ג'ובס לא הייתה טכנולוגית אלא עסקית - המשא ומתן עם חברות התקליטים כדי למכור כל שיר ב-99 סנט ב-iTunes. זה היה ה-enabler שאפשר את ההצלחה הגדולה של האיפוד.

שטרן מדגיש שרוב החברות המצליחות בעולם לא המציאו טכנולוגיה מהפכנית. מיקרוסופט קנתה את מערכת ההפעלה DOS, פייסבוק וטוויטר לא פיתחו טכנולוגיות חדשות, ואפילו אנבידיה הצליחה בזכות שימוש חכם בטכנולוגיה קיימת. המפתח להצלחה הוא זיהוי של enablers - טכנולוגיות או החלטות עסקיות שהופכות לזמינות ופותחות הזדמנויות חדשות. דוגמאות לכך כוללות זיהוי דיבור לטקסט, תרגום אוטומטי, זיהוי פנים, ובינה מלאכותית. כאשר מזהים enabler ומשלבים אותו עם הבנה עמוקה של Jobs to be Done בשוק ספציפי, אפשר ליצור פתרונות מצליחים ללא צורך בהשקעה עצומה במחקר ופיתוח. המסקנה היא שהצלחה עסקית נובעת מהבנת הלקוח והשוק, ולא בהכרח מחדשנות טכנולוגית.
